source.title: Weight Expansion: A New Perspective on Dropout and Generalization
source.authors: Gao Jin; Xin-Ping Yi; Peng-Fei Yang; Li-Jun Zhang; S. Schewe; Xiaowei Huang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is supplied
record.tranche_reason: Tests dropout’s effect on generalization with loss-gap and accuracy-gap measures, and relates weight volume to the gap; it does not test the original versions’ random-label, width, architecture comparison, optimizer, batch-size, or magnitude-aware sharpness claims.
record.gate_note: Rows report the paper’s own dropout-versus-no-dropout results and its dropout-rate sweep. Cited findings from other work and complexity measures used only to compare prediction of the generalization gap are not recorded as results. The paper’s weight-volume results do not measure the magnitude-aware sharpness in V7.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares held-out classification accuracy with and without dropout in Appendix J and Table 13, testing V6. The extracted generalization-gap rows alone cannot establish lower held-out error: a smaller gap can result from worse training performance.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's central paraphrase is accurate: the authors argue that dropout expands weight volume, that expansion indicates reduced generalization error, and that dropout provides an inexpensive way to obtain it. The record's claimed text-classification metric conflict is incorrect: Table 13 shows both loss and accuracy gaps decreasing. The authors' broad improvement language also overlooks the small test-accuracy decreases in two VGG16 conditions.
record.recipe_differences: Studies dropout’s effect on generalization through weight-volume estimates and loss or accuracy gaps; it does not reproduce the original dropout study’s comparisons or test its small-training-set and joint-removal qualifications.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported dropout-rate sweep shows the gap decreasing as the rate increases from 0.0 to 0.45 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The paper also notes that rates close to 1 seriously reduce training accuracy. On THUCNews, loss gaps rise under dropout while accuracy gaps fall.

fits_no_version.finding: Dropout reduces the reported loss gaps across the image experiments and all three text classifiers; the rate sweep also reduces gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dropout can reduce test-minus-training loss, which does not by itself establish lower held-out classification error.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight-volume measures predict generalization gaps better than the tested isotropic sharpness and norm measures.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Covariance-aware PAC-Bayes complexity measures can improve prediction of generalization gaps in the tested dropout networks.

fits_no_version.finding: TextRNN test accuracy increases from 0.9037 to 0.9102 with dropout.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dropout improves held-out accuracy for the tested recurrent text classifier.

record.problems: The paper itself notes that large dropout rates can seriously reduce training accuracy and says it therefore considers rates only in [0, 0.45]. Its text-classification results are metric-dependent: loss gaps increase while accuracy gaps decrease. The sampling estimates in tables report ± values, but most generalization-gap comparisons do not report uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the listed versions were reported beyond the extracted dropout and generalization-gap results. The paper’s complexity-measure mutual-information comparisons and weight-volume measurements were not given separate rows because they do not measure the specific behaviors in V1–V8; the weight-volume/generalization association is summarized under fits_no_version.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out accuracy.
Held-out error when widening beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizer comparisons and tuning qualifications.
Batch-size penalties under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.

Very small training sets and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation. Excessive-dropout underfitting is discussed but not experimentally measured; experiments restrict rates to 0–0.45.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. The tested isotropic sharpness and weight-volume measures do not instantiate this version.
Removal of highly memorized training examples versus random removal.

missing.what: Direct test-accuracy comparisons for VGG11 and VGG16 on CIFAR-10/100 without weight decay, including the VGG16 CIFAR-10 decrease.
Direct test-accuracy comparisons for VGG11 and VGG16 on CIFAR-10/100 with weight decay 0.0005, including the VGG16 CIFAR-100 decrease.
Top-1 and top-5 test accuracies for VGG11 and VGG16 on ImageNet-32, with weight decay 0 and 0.0005.
FastText and TextCNN held-out accuracies with and without dropout.
Dropout-versus-normal test-loss curves for VGG16 and AlexNet on ImageNet-32, CIFAR-100, CIFAR-10 and SVHN. The text describes improvement, but exact curve values are unavailable in the supplied text.

record.verdict_notes: A generalization gap and held-out classification error are distinct outcomes. All extracted rows measure gaps, so V6 verdicts rely on explicitly identified missing accuracy rows. No verdict is assigned to V7 because neither isotropic perturbations nor covariance volume measures weight-magnitude-scaled sharpness.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and optimizer tuning.
Large-batch versus small-batch training and recipe changes.
The paper does not report dropout results on very small training sets or test joint removal of dropout and weight decay with data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.
